name: mlpack
baseline: scikit-learn (sklearn); the same tables also compare Shogun Toolkit, MATLAB, Weka and mlpy
workload: Wall-clock seconds for k-nearest-neighbors (k=3) and k-means (same starting centroids, 1000 iterations max) on ten data sets (eight UCI sets, MNIST 70000x784, a uniform random 1000000x10 set), mlpack 1.0.3 against the libraries' contemporary releases; load time excluded, mean of 5 runs.
claimed_speedup: Paper states mlpack k-NN and k-means are 'faster than the competitors in all test cases'. k-NN seconds, mlpack vs sklearn: isolet 13.0197 vs 46.8016, miniboone 20.2045 vs 714.2385 (about 35x, derived from page data), covtype 14.3449 vs 651.6259, corel 4.9716 vs 160.4597, randu 1020.9142 vs 8780.0176; Weka isolet 213.4735. k-means seconds: randu 727.1498 vs Shogun 7443.2675, MATLAB 3117.5177, sklearn 'memory' (out of memory); isolet 4.9762 vs sklearn 7.0902; miniboone 0.1853 vs MATLAB 0.7221, sklearn out of memory.
hardware: AMD Phenom II X6 1100T at 3.3 GHz, 8 GB RAM (single consumer workstation)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 library that needs Armadillo plus a BLAS/LAPACK (OpenBLAS pthreads builds 0.3.26 and older can oversubscribe threads, per the README warning); template-heavy so compile time and memory are high unless individual headers are included; bindings for Python, Julia, Go, R and CLI.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (JMLR 14, 2013, machine learning open source software track, four pages) but written by mlpack's own developers. Numbers are from 2012-era releases (mlpack 1.0.3; competitor versions are not stated in the paper) on a 2011 CPU, so they say little about today's scikit-learn. Only k-NN and k-means are tabulated; 'other methods, omitted due to space constraints' are asserted to show similar speedups. Compiler and flags are not stated in the paper (benchmark scripts are public at github.com/mlpack/benchmarks, so a rerun is possible but no CPU/flags match is documented), which is why this is B and not A. mlpack's k-NN uses tree-based exact search while some competitors ran brute force or other settings. The live results page mlpack.org/benchmark.html and the later benchmark system paper (2014automatic.pdf) carry no numbers that could be opened here. The 2018 and 2023 JOSS papers contain no performance numbers except that compilation is 'often an order of magnitude faster' after dropping Boost. No comparison against TensorFlow or PyTorch exists in these sources.
found_via: seed-record pass; lead was the awesome-cpp Machine Learning entry for mlpack. Started from the mlpack README, then the website repo's papers folder (https://github.com/mlpack/mlpack.org/tree/master/papers) where 2013mlpack.pdf was fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: ODE (Open Dynamics Engine)
baseline: Bullet Physics (through Gazebo-classic's Bullet plugin); the same benchmark also runs DART and Simbody
workload: Real-time factor (wall-clock time divided by simulated time, lower is faster) of rigid-body simulation inside Gazebo-classic: a stack of boxes with large inertia ratio (object-stacking benchmark), and free-floating 1x4x9 boxes, 1 to 101 boxes at 0.0005 s step.
claimed_speedup: ROSCon 2014 slide 16 (Benchmark 3, object stacking), time ratio real/sim: ODE 0.4, Bullet 0.5, DART 1.1, Simbody >100 (ODE about 1.25x faster than Bullet, derived from page data). Result CSV test_results/BENCHMARK_boxes_model_count.csv (timeRatio, dt 0.0005): 1 box ODE 0.101879 vs Bullet 0.127279 (collision flag 0) and 0.109099 vs 0.129334 (flag 1); 101 boxes ODE 1.3357 vs Bullet 1.4384 (flag 1, 1.08x derived) but ODE 1.58186 vs Bullet 1.47622 (flag 0, ODE about 7% slower).
stars_or_usage: 30 stars on the new GitHub home (project moved from Bitbucket odedevs/ode in 2026); physics backend supported by Gazebo-classic
tradeoffs: Maximal-coordinates rigid-body engine with impulse/iterative (quickstep) contact solver and built-in collision detection; favours speed and stability over physical accuracy; the benchmark's accuracy columns show ODE and Bullet at similar error levels for the box test (energy error 0.0062 vs 0.0068 for one box).
caveats: Independent measurement (Gazebo maintainer's physics benchmark, shown at ROSCon 2014 and Multibody 2015) but the repo has 16 stars, no CPU model, compiler or flags are stated, and the CSV results are dated about 2014-2015. The summary slide notes implicit joint damping exists only 'in our fork of ODE' (OSRF's Gazebo fork), so the ODE measured may be that fork rather than upstream; both engines run through Gazebo-classic wrappers so Gazebo overhead is included. The slide numbers are rounded to one decimal and sit next to a stack-position-error plot in which Bullet's error is lower than ODE's at the lighter top-link masses, so the stacking speed result is not accuracy-matched. Result is mixed: ODE is faster than Bullet in 10 of 12 box-count configurations (by 4 to 25%) but 3.5 to 7% slower at 81 and 101 boxes with collision flag 0. The benchmark's ODE and Bullet step sizes match (0.0005 s) but Simbody used 0.001 s. The peer-reviewed Erez et al. ICRA 2015 comparison of Bullet, Havok, MuJoCo, ODE and PhysX and the Boeing and Braunl engine comparison exist but could not be opened (hosts blocked), and by search summary no engine wins everywhere. ODE's own site (ode.org) was blocked and its README gives only the words 'fast, flexible, robust' with no numbers.
found_via: seed-record pass; lead was the ode.org entry in awesome-cpp (blocked here). Bitbucket README (https://bitbucket.org/odedevs/ode/src/master/README.md) pointed to the new GitHub home; WebSearch for physics engine comparisons led to https://github.com/scpeters/benchmark.

name: oneDAL (oneAPI Data Analytics Library)
baseline: scikit-learn 1.8.0 (stock CPU implementation); the oneDAL README separately compares against Apache Spark MLlib
workload: Training (fit) and inference (predict/transform) time per scikit-learn estimator, Extension for Scikit-learn (sklearnex 2026.0.0, which calls oneDAL) against stock scikit-learn 1.8.0, combined FP32 and FP64 averages on one socket of a Xeon 6767P; oneDAL README adds Implicit ALS, K-means, linear regression, correlation and PCA against Apache Spark MLlib on 7 x AWS m5.2xlarge.
claimed_speedup: sklearnex README text: 'average speed up of 8.5x on training and inference', 'up to 100X'. README chart image (scikit-learn-acceleration.PNG): fit LinearRegression 48.5x, SVR 28.8x, Ridge 15.2x, SVC 14.6x, KMeans 7.7x, DBSCAN 3.0x, ElasticNet 1.2x, Lasso 1.1x; predict SVC 236.3x, SVR 330.5x, KMeans 24.6x, ElasticNet 1.1x. oneDAL README: '3-18x increase in performance compared to the default Apache Spark MLlib' (chart: Implicit ALS 3.6x, K-means 7.4x, Linear Regression 13.8x, Correlation 18.1x, PCA 18.2x).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated; prebuilt packages: Python 3.12.13, NumPy 2.4.4, pandas 3.0.2, SciPy 1.17.1, scikit-learn 1.8.0, scikit-learn-intelex 2026.0.0, Ubuntu 24.04.3, kernel 6.8.0-47; run with numactl --physcpubind=0-63 --membind=0,1
hardware: 1 node, 6th Gen Intel Xeon 6767P, 64 cores per socket, 2 sockets (1 used), HT on, Turbo on, SNC on, 1024 GB DDR5-8800; tested by Intel as of 2026-06-01. Spark chart: 7 x m5.2xlarge AWS instances (CPU model not given).
stars_or_usage: 652 stars; powers scikit-learn-intelex (1.4k stars) and OAP MLlib; UXL Foundation project (moved from oneapi-src/oneDAL)
tradeoffs: Intel-led, x86 SIMD and cache tuning for CPUs plus SYCL GPU and MPI distributed modes; results are 'equivalent mathematical accuracy' rather than bit-identical to scikit-learn; some estimators gain little (ElasticNet, Lasso, brute-force KNN regressor fit about 1.0 to 1.2x).
caveats: First-party Intel numbers on Intel hardware, not peer reviewed, so C. The speedup is measured through the Python sklearnex wrapper on stock scikit-learn, not through oneDAL's C++ API. Benchmark code is linked (github.com/IntelPython/scikit-learn_bench, Apache-2.0, 124 stars) but its README does not say which configs or data sizes produced the chart, and no compiler or flags are given, so it is short of A. The 8.5x average and 'up to 100X' are README text; the per-algorithm values were read from the chart image in the README. The Spark MLlib chart is older (Intel DAAL 2020 Gold, Spark 2.4.4, emr-5.27.0, double precision, no benchmark code, no CPU model). The old repo URL https://github.com/oneapi-src/oneDAL now lives at uxlfoundation/oneDAL. The arXiv 1909.11822 scaling paper cited by the README was not opened (arxiv.org blocked).
found_via: seed-record pass; lead was the awesome-cpp Machine Learning entry for oneDAL. Started from the oneDAL README (raw.githubusercontent.com/oneapi-src/oneDAL), then the scikit-learn-intelex README and its acceleration chart.
